position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium professional quality, convenience, and modern design, targeting home office and small retail segments. Use the existing Franke brand and distribution channels to reach individual buyers directly, leveraging the professional reputation to justify premium pricing.

frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be evaluated against the cost of development, distribution, and potential return on investment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, or travel) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., semi‑automatic machines for home use) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional coffee machines and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Franke's own brand.

X1.name: Premium vs Eco‑Certified Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a Franke coffee machine (identical spec‑s) and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested). The description is presented with one of two messaging frames: (A) premium‑focused (highlighting professional quality, convenience, and modern design) or (B) eco‑focused (highlighting water‑saving, carbon‑neutral, and sustainable materials). Randomly assigned to either frame.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in Germany and Switzerland, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Stratify by home‑coffee‑machine purchase frequency (annual) to capture both occasional and frequent buyers.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) for each messaging condition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be evaluated against the cost of development, distribution, and potential return on investment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, or travel) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., semi‑automatic machines for home use) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional coffee machines and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Franke's own brand.

T1.claim: Home office workers treat coffee machines as a productivity tool. They would purchase a machine that automates brewing, saves time, and offers consistent quality, even if it is a larger, more expensive device than a traditional drip coffee maker.
T1.who_benefits: Home office workers gain time savings and consistent coffee quality, while Franke gains higher-margin sales of a differentiated consumer product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising remote work has increased demand for convenience and consistency in coffee preparation, making workers willing to pay for automation and premium features.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Franke would capture value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and potential subscription services for maintenance or loyalty programs.

They are willing to pay a premium for time-saving automation.
Franke can produce and distribute a differentiated consumer product within the budget.
predictions: A survey of home office workers would show that a majority would purchase a home coffee machine for time savings.
Sales data would show higher sales volume in regions with high remote work penetration.
Customers would express willingness to pay a premium price for automation features.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Home Office vs Lifestyle Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 home office workers (remote work, 1-5 years) and 250 lifestyle-conscious consumers (age 25-45, high disposable income). Recruit via panel providers.
X1.measure: 1) Percentage of respondents choosing the home office proposition (T1) vs the lifestyle proposition (T2). 2) Average WTP premium over a baseline (e.g., €200) for each proposition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home office group will choose the home office proposition at ≥55% and show WTP premium ≥€150 over baseline.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle group will choose the lifestyle proposition at ≥55% and show WTP premium ≥€150 over baseline.

X1.decision_rule: If the home office group’s share exceeds the lifestyle group by ≥5 percentage points and its WTP premium is ≥€150, proceed with a differentiated home‑office proposition. If the lifestyle group’s share exceeds by ≥5 points and its WTP premium is ≥€150, proceed with a lifestyle proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

Participants are asked to indicate their primary purchase reason (convenience vs cost savings) and willingness to pay a premium.
X1.sample: 500 residential consumers (aged 25-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions.
X1.measure: Primary purchase reason (convenience vs cost savings) and willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay at least 10% more than a standard commercial unit).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Condition A.

If both conditions are equal, do not invest in a differentiated proposition at this time.

X1.name: Differentiated vs Branded Ice Machine Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a differentiated ice machine (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling) or a branded ice machine (e.g., Scotsman Brilliance). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults aged 25–45 who have purchased an ice machine in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the differentiated unit than for the branded unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the branded unit than for the differentiated unit.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the differentiated and branded units is at least 1.5 points (e.g., differentiated intent ≥ 7.5 and branded intent ≤ 6), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is at least 1.5 points in favor of the branded unit, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., nugget ice or easy refilling) rather than a brand-led premium offering. The evidence shows existing consumer interest in countertop ice machines and the ability to differentiate through convenience and novelty, which aligns with T1.
final.target_customer: Home consumers aged 25–45 who have purchased an ice machine in the past 12 months and seek convenience, novelty, or a better ice experience.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated ice machine that delivers a unique, convenient experience (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling) that cannot be obtained from existing commercial or generic models, allowing Hoshizaki to capture value through licensing, premium
final.next_action: Run the proposed differentiated vs branded ice machine test (500 U.S. adults, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the differentiated unit shows a ≥1.5‑point advantage, proceed to develop and launch the
final.uncertainty: The willingness of consumers to pay a premium for convenience and novelty is uncertain. The test will resolve this, but current evidence does not definitively show demand for nugget ice or brand premium pricing.
would_change_if: If the test shows the branded unit outperforming the differentiated unit by ≥1.5 points, we would shift focus to a brand-led premium proposition.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for nugget ice or brand reputation driving purchases, we would reconsider the differentiated approach.

arguments.name: Differentiated vs Branded Ice Machine Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a differentiated ice machine (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling) or a branded ice machine (e.g., Scotsman Brilliance). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults aged 25–45 who have purchased an ice machine in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the differentiated unit than for the branded unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the branded unit than for the differentiated unit.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the differentiated and branded units is at least 1.5 points (e.g., differentiated intent ≥ 7.5 and branded intent ≤ 6), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is at least 1.5 points in favor of the branded unit, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

X1.name: Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) convenience-driven home ice machine (nugget ice, on-demand convenience) or (B) commercial-grade fleet unit (high output, reliability, service). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the primary reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 300 residential consumers (150 per condition) and 200 commercial buyers (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of convenience for the convenience message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of commercial output for the commercial message.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience message is at least 1.5 points higher than for the commercial message (i.e., >= 5.5 out of 7) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If both conditions show similar intent, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand drivers or willingness to pay for home ice machines. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential home ice machines, emphasizing convenience, nugget ice, and on-demand access. This aligns with evidence of consumer demand for countertop formats and the existence of a dedicated consumer category (Scotsman Brilliance).
final.target_customer: Residential consumers seeking convenient, high-quality ice for beverages and food preparation.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced countertop home ice machine that delivers consistent, chewable nugget ice with advanced features (smart controls, energy efficiency) and easy installation, leveraging Hoshizaki’s brand and distribution network.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay for the convenience-driven proposition.

If new evidence shows strong demand from commercial buyers (e.g., high-output units) or a clear willingness to pay premium for commercial features, the recommendation would shift toward a commercial‑

arguments.claim: Home ice maker demand is driven by convenience and the desire for fresh, chewable ice, not by a need for commercial-grade output. arguments.who_benefits: Residential consumers seeking convenient, high-quality ice for beverages and food preparation.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from buying ice from stores or using ice tongs to owning a dedicated home machine because it eliminates the hassle and provides consistent, chewable ice on demand.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki can capture value by selling premium-priced countertop models with advanced features (e.g., nugget ice, smart controls) through direct sales and retail channels, leveraging its existing brand and distribution network.
assumptions: Consumers perceive home ice machines as a convenience product rather than a commercial-grade fleet item.
Willingness to pay exceeds the cost of a standard commercial unit due to convenience and brand perception.
Distribution channels (direct sales, retail) can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: A survey of residential consumers would show a higher purchase intent for a home ice machine than for a commercial-grade fleet unit.
Sales of premium-priced countertop models would exceed sales of standard commercial units in the same market.
Consumer reviews would emphasize convenience and taste as primary purchase drivers.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These buyers shift from using ice tongs or store-bought ice to owning a dedicated machine because it reduces labor costs, ensures consistent product quality, and meets regulatory or service standards.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki can capture value by offering high-output, durable commercial units with advanced service support, and by selling through existing commercial distribution channels.
assumptions: Commercial buyers prioritize output capacity and reliability over convenience.
There is a measurable demand for units that can serve multiple points of service.
Service and maintenance capabilities are critical to purchase decisions.
predictions: A survey of commercial buyers would show higher purchase intent for high-output units than for premium-priced countertop models.
Sales of commercial-grade fleet units would exceed sales of premium-priced consumer models in the same market.
Buyers would emphasize serviceability and maintenance support as key purchase criteria.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) convenience-driven home ice machine (nugget ice, on-demand convenience) or (B) commercial-grade fleet unit (high output, reliability, service). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the primary reason for choosing the product.
arguments.sample: 300 residential consumers (150 per condition) and 200 commercial buyers (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of convenience for the convenience message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of commercial output for the commercial message.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience message is at least 1.5 points higher than for the commercial message (i.e., >= 5.5 out of 7) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If both conditions show similar intent, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential home ice machines, emphasizing convenience, nugget ice, and on-demand access. This aligns with evidence of consumer demand for countertop formats and the existence of a dedicated consumer category (Scotsman Brilliance).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hoshizaki Corporation investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machines, portable refrigerators, or specialized kitchen equipment).

X1.name: Differentiated Ice Machine Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a differentiated ice machine (e.g., chewable ice, easy refilling) and a standard refrigerator ice unit. They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. They also indicate whether they would purchase based on convenience (T1) or a specific pain point (T2).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a typical home market.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the differentiated ice machine than for the standard refrigerator ice unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the differentiated ice machine that explicitly addresses a pain point (e.g., water waste, ice quality, space constraints) than for the standard refrigerator ice unit.

X1.decision_rule: If the differentiated ice machine achieves a purchase intent score at least 10 points higher than the standard refrigerator ice unit and its maximum price is at least 20% above the standard unit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 10 points or the price premium is less than 20%, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address consumer demand for convenience or willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated ice machine. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.value_proposition: A differentiated ice machine that delivers a unique, convenient experience (e.g., chewable ice, easy refilling) that standard refrigerators cannot provide, allowing Hoshizaki to capture premium pricing and brand loyalty.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12‑week, €20,000 online survey test comparing purchase intent and maximum price willingness to pay for a differentiated ice machine versus a standard refrigerator ice unit, using the decision rule to decide on investment.
final.uncertainty: Whether consumers will pay a premium for convenience and whether convenience is the primary driver of purchase. The test will resolve this uncertainty.

arguments.name: Differentiated Ice Machine Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a differentiated ice machine (e.g., chewable ice, easy refilling) and a standard refrigerator ice unit. They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. They also indicate whether they would purchase based on convenience (T1) or a specific pain point (T2).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a typical home market.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the differentiated ice machine than for the standard refrigerator ice unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the differentiated ice machine that explicitly addresses a pain point (e.g., water waste, ice quality, space constraints) than for the standard refrigerator ice unit.

arguments.decision_rule: If the differentiated ice machine achieves a purchase intent score at least 10 points higher than the standard refrigerator ice unit and its maximum price is at least 20% above the standard unit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 10 points or the price premium is less than 20%, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hoshizaki Corporation investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machines, portable refrigerators, or specialized kitchen equipment).
2) Expand the existing commercial product line into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., broader distribution of current commercial products).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment business.
4) Change the route to buyers or customer group (e.g., shift from direct sales to retail partnerships or target a different demographic) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Home consumers will adopt a differentiated ice machine if it offers a unique convenience feature (e.g., chewable ice, easy refilling) that cannot be obtained from existing commercial units.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking convenient, delicious ice at home; Hoshizaki benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently buy commercial ice machines for fleet or large-scale use; a differentiated feature creates a new use case that justifies higher purchase cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki can price the differentiated unit above standard commercial units and sell through retail channels, earning margin on a new consumer segment.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a feature that improves convenience.
Hoshizaki can design and manufacture a differentiated unit without compromising commercial performance.
Retail distribution exists for a consumer-oriented unit.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated ice machine will generate higher purchase intent or sales than a standard commercial unit.
Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as the top reason for choosing the differentiated unit.

T2.claim: Home consumers will adopt a differentiated ice machine if it offers a unique feature that addresses a specific pain point (e.g., water conservation, energy efficiency) that commercial units do not.
T2.who_benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers; Hoshizaki benefits by positioning as an eco-friendly brand and potentially accessing new market segments.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers are increasingly motivated by sustainability; a feature that reduces water or energy use creates a tangible benefit that justifies a premium purchase.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki can price the differentiated unit higher and market it as an eco-friendly product, capturing margin through a new consumer segment.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces water or energy consumption.

predictions: A test offering an eco-featured ice machine will show higher purchase intent among environmentally conscious consumers than a standard commercial unit.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small‑business owners, emphasizing convenience, compact size, and low upfront cost. Begin with a limited retail launch and gather real‑world purchase intent data before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Tennant.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential home cleaning, small‑business cleaning, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand the existing professional product line with new features or packaging without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., premium branding, new accessories).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current professional market and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, subscription model, or partnership with retail chains) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small‑business owners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they increasingly view floor cleaning as a chore they can automate and because they value convenience and lower upfront cost, so a manufacturer that can deliver a compact, easy‑to‑use machine at a price they can afford will capture value through higher volume sales.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who need to clean hard floors without a full mopping system.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from manual mopping to a machine that does the work, reducing time and effort, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that fits their space and budget.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would sell a compact, low‑cost scrubber directly to consumers through retail channels, earning margin on each unit sold.
assumptions: Consumers currently avoid purchasing floor‑cleaning machines due to cost or perceived complexity.
A compact, easy‑to‑use machine meets the functional need of homeowners and small‑business owners.
Retail distribution can reach the target consumer base.
predictions: If offered a compact scrubber priced under $300, at least 10% of surveyed homeowners and small‑business owners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher in regions with higher home‑owning rates and lower average household income.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from using multiple tools to a single, reliable machine that reduces downtime and labor costs, and they are willing to pay a premium for durability and performance.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would sell a professional‑grade scrubber through distributors at a higher margin, leveraging its existing distribution network to reach contractors.

A durable, high‑performance machine reduces downtime and labor costs.
Distributors are willing to stock a professional‑grade product at a premium price.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent in Group A is at least 15 percentage points higher than in Group B, conclude T1 is supported. X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Cleaning Proposition
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners and small business owners. They are shown two product descriptions of a differentiated consumer floor-cleaning machine (e.g., a compact scrubber for small spaces). One description emphasizes premium positioning (e.g., 'Convenient, high-performance cleaning for small areas') and the other emphasizes safety-critical features (e.g., 'Child-safe, slip-resistant design for safe home cleaning'). Participants are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Sustainability
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a compact, high-performance scrubber marketed as convenient for small spaces and tight budgets. Group B sees the same product described as sustainable, eco-friendly, and water-efficient. Both groups see price points and a call-to-action to purchase. The test measures purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (maximum price).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two groups (150 per group). Recruitment targets homeowners and small business owners with limited space.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated primary purchase driver (convenience vs sustainability).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A purchase intent exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points and its average willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, conclude T1 is supported. If Group B purchase intent exceeds Group A by at least 10 percentage points and its average willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Sustainability
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a compact, high-performance scrubber marketed as convenient for small spaces and tight budgets. Group B sees the same product described as sustainable, eco-friendly, and water-efficient. Both groups see price points and a call-to-action to purchase. The test measures purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (maximum price).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two groups (150 per group). Recruitment targets homeowners and small business owners with limited space.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated primary purchase driver (convenience vs sustainability).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A purchase intent exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points and its average willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, conclude T1 is supported. If Group B purchase intent exceeds Group A by at least 10 percentage points and its average willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience, small-space performance, and budget-friendly pricing. The evidence shows existing consumer sales and a product (T360) positioned for tight budgets, but no direct proof of consumer willingness to pay a premium. Conduct a targeted test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing to full-scale development.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and ease of use for small spaces, leveraging existing retail distribution to reach homeowners and small‑business owners. The evidence shows a consumer channel split and a product designed for smaller areas, but no direct proof of consumer willingness to pay a premium. Conduct a low‑cost test to validate demand before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Tennant.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential home cleaning, small‑business cleaning, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand the existing professional product line with new features or packaging without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., premium branding, new accessories).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current professional market and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, subscription model, or partnership with retail chains) without altering the product.

assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and ease of use.

The product can be marketed as a premium, convenient solution distinct from professional equipment.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium, safety-focused sustainability and environmental benefits, targeting homeowners and small‑business owners who value eco‑friendly cleaning solutions. Use the premium positioning to justify higher margins and sell through specialty retailers or online channels that highlight sustainability.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Tennant.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential home cleaning, small‑business cleaning, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand the existing professional product line with new features or packaging without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., premium branding, new accessories).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current professional market and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, subscription model, or partnership with retail chains) without altering the product.

T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who value eco‑friendly, low‑maintenance cleaning equipment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing environmental awareness and concerns about water waste make consumers willing to pay more for products that offer a measurable environmental benefit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value by pricing the product at a premium, selling through specialty retailers or online channels, and leveraging the brand association with sustainability to justify higher margins.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for eco‑friendly cleaning solutions.
Environmental messaging effectively influences purchase decisions.
Tennant can effectively communicate the sustainability benefits of its products.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced eco‑friendly floor scrubber, at least 30% of respondents will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher in regions with higher environmental awareness scores compared to regions with lower awareness.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Busy consumers prioritize products that reduce effort and provide quick results, making convenience a primary purchase driver.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value by offering a compact, easy‑to‑use product with clear instructions and support, and by selling through retail channels that emphasize convenience and quick results.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a product that saves time and effort.
Convenience messaging effectively differentiates the product from competitors.
Retail distribution can effectively highlight the product's ease of use.
predictions: In a test offering a compact, easy‑to‑use floor scrubber, at least 25% of respondents will report intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion will be higher in regions where time‑saving is a top concern compared to regions where other factors dominate.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions of a compact, eco‑friendly floor scrubber. Participants are randomly assigned to view either the premium‑sustainability description or the convenience‑time‑saving description. After viewing, they are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and income to ensure representation of both premium‑priced and budget‑conscious segments.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the premium‑sustainability description compared to the convenience description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the convenience‑time‑saving description compared to the premium description.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium‑sustainability description achieves a purchase intent score of at least 7.5 and a maximum price of at least $150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing sustainability. If the convenience description achieves a purchase intent score of at least 7.5 and a maximum price of at least $150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on the current professional market.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium, safety-focused sustainability and environmental benefits, targeting homeowners and small‑business owners who value eco‑friendly cleaning solutions. Use the premium positioning to justify higher margins and sell through specialty retailers or online channels that highlight sustainability.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small‑business owners who prioritize eco‑friendly, low‑maintenance cleaning equipment.
final.value_proposition: A premium, safety‑focused floor scrubber that reduces water use, provides a health‑conscious cleaning experience, and delivers superior performance in smaller spaces, positioned as a sustainable home cleaning solution.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 U.S. adults, 12‑week timeline, €20,000 budget) to validate purchase intent and price willingness for the premium‑sustainability versus convenience messaging.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a premium eco‑friendly product and the relative importance of sustainability versus convenience are uncertain. Consumer demand for such a product is not directly evidenced in public sources.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 7.5 or maximum price below $150 for the premium‑sustainability description, indicating insufficient consumer demand, the recommendation would shift to no expansion and continued focus on the current
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for convenience‑driven products, the recommendation would shift to emphasizing convenience over sustainability.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions of a compact, eco‑friendly floor scrubber. Participants are randomly assigned to view either the premium‑sustainability description or the convenience‑time‑saving description. After viewing, they are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and income to ensure representation of both premium‑priced and budget‑conscious segments.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the premium‑sustainability description compared to the convenience description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the convenience‑time‑saving description compared to the premium description.

arguments.decision_rule: If the premium‑sustainability description achieves a purchase intent score of at least 7.5 and a maximum price of at least $150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing sustainability. If the convenience description achieves a purchase intent score of at least 7.5 and a maximum price of at least $150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on the current professional market.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium, safety-focused sustainability and environmental benefits, targeting homeowners and small‑business owners who value eco‑friendly cleaning solutions. Use the premium positioning to justify higher margins and sell through specialty retailers or online channels that highlight sustainability.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Belimo’s existing B2B business model and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential home automation, DIY HVAC control, or a new consumer segment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new features or packaging without targeting consumers directly.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from generic thermostats or off-brand devices to a Belimo product because they associate Belimo with high-quality, low-maintenance commercial HVAC components.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo would sell premium-priced residential control systems directly or through specialty retailers, capturing higher margins than bulk OEM sales.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a product marketed as safety-critical for HVAC systems.

There is a measurable segment of homeowners who currently lack reliable residential HVAC control.
predictions: In a test offering a Belimo residential zone control system at a price 20% above a comparable generic thermostat, purchase intent among homeowners will be at least 15% higher than for a generic alternative.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Belimo’s existing B2B business model and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential home automation, DIY HVAC control, or a new consumer segment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new features or packaging without targeting consumers directly.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with home‑im improvement retailers, or a subscription model for home control services).

assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for energy-efficient HVAC solutions.
Regulatory incentives or consumer awareness campaigns further drive demand.
Belimo can effectively communicate energy savings benefits to consumers.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics or lifestyle brands for consumer devices.

T1.claim: Home CPR training increases public awareness and willingness to intervene in cardiac arrest, leading individuals to purchase home training kits to prepare for emergencies. The perceived reduction of risk and the ability to act immediately create demand, which Laerdal can capture through direct-to-consumer sales of portable kits.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who need to prepare for emergencies, and by extension, bystanders who might perform CPR in an emergency.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased public awareness of the importance of bystander CPR and the availability of easy-to-use home kits lowers the perceived risk and creates a perceived benefit, prompting individuals to own the training device.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal would capture value through premium-priced home CPR kits sold directly to consumers, generating revenue beyond B2B training programs.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of the importance of bystander CPR and are willing to invest in home training.
Home CPR kits are perceived as safe and effective for self-training.
Laerdal can reach and convert consumers effectively at a price point that justifies the investment.
predictions: In regions with high public awareness of bystander CPR, home CPR kit purchases will be higher than in regions with low awareness.
Consumers will indicate a willingness to pay a premium for a home CPR kit compared to a standard CPR manikin.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Emergency vs Wellness Framing
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel representing health-conscious and general consumers. Participants view a product description of a portable home CPR kit and are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) Emergency preparedness framing (emphasizes bystander CPR, life-saving skills, and family preparedness). (B) Wellness framing (emphasizes personal health, fitness, and lifestyle integration). After viewing the description, participants indicate their willingness to pay a premium (price sensitivity) and their intent to purchase (binary).
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited from a health-conscious panel and a general consumer panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay premium (difference in price sensitivity between conditions) and purchase intent (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent in the emergency framing condition compared to wellness framing.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent in the wellness framing condition compared to emergency framing.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay premium for emergency framing exceeds wellness framing by at least €10 (or a 10% increase in purchase intent), proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on emergency preparedness. If the difference is less than €10, the test is inconclusive and further market research is needed.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, focusing on emergency preparedness messaging. The evidence shows a growing trend of bystander CPR participation in public cases, and Laerdal already offers a consumer product (CPR Anytime) that can be enhanced with targeted marketing. The proposed test can validate whether emergency framing drives higher willingness to pay and purchase intent.

final.value_proposition: A portable home CPR kit marketed as a lifesaving emergency preparedness tool, enabling individuals to learn CPR at their own pace and share the training with family members, thereby increasing overall public preparedness.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics or lifestyle brands for consumer devices.

X1.name: Home CPR Training Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 500 homeowners (300 per arm) who have expressed interest in home safety products. Randomly assign participants to one of two messaging conditions: (A) safety/ preparedness message emphasizing personal preparedness for home emergencies; (B) compliance/ insurance message emphasizing meeting insurance or employer requirements. After viewing a product description, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners (300 per arm) screened via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each messaging condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the safety/ preparedness condition compared to the compliance condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the compliance/ insurance condition compared to the safety condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the safety condition is at least 10 points higher than in the compliance condition (i.e., safety ≥ compliance + 10), proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on personal preparedness. If compliance ≥ safety + 10, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on insurance/ employer compliance. If neither condition meets the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Laerdal already offers home CPR training (CPR Anytime) and donates infant kits, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand or willingness to pay. The proposed messaging test (X1) is the next step to validate whether safety/ preparedness messaging drives purchase intent.
final.target_customer: Homeowners who have expressed interest in home safety products and are concerned about home cardiac emergencies.
final.value_proposition: A home CPR training kit positioned as a personal preparedness product, offering flexible, at-home learning with optional family training resources.
final.next_action: Run the Home CPR Training Messaging Test (X1) to compare purchase intent and willingness to pay under safety/ preparedness versus compliance/ insurance messaging.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home CPR training and the actual willingness to pay are unknown. The test will resolve whether safety/ preparedness messaging drives demand.
would_change_if: If the messaging test shows the compliance/ insurance condition achieving purchase intent at least 10 points higher than the safety condition, we would shift focus to an insurance/ employer compliance proposition.
If neither condition meets the threshold, we would conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment in a differentiated consumer proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). They are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) Personal health responsibility messaging (emphasizing individual preparedness and family safety); (2) Health routine integration messaging (emphasizing convenience and alignment with existing health habits); (3) Authority endorsement messaging (emphasizing endorsement by trusted health authorities). Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay for the product.
X1.sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three conditions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for the home CPR training kit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the personal health responsibility condition compared to the other two conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the health routine integration condition compared to the other two conditions.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the personal health responsibility condition is at least 10 points higher than in the health routine integration condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on personal health responsibility. If the average purchase intent in the health routine integration condition is at least 10 points higher than in the personal health responsibility condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T2 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health routine integration. If neither condition shows a significant difference, the recommendation is to maintain the current B2B focus.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). They are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) Personal health responsibility messaging (emphasizing individual preparedness and family safety); (2) Health routine integration messaging (emphasizing convenience and alignment with existing health habits); (3) Authority endorsement messaging (emphasizing endorsement by trusted health authorities). Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay for the product.
arguments.sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three conditions.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for the home CPR training kit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the personal health responsibility condition compared to the other two conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the health routine integration condition compared to the other two conditions.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the personal health responsibility condition is at least 10 points higher than in the health routine integration condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on personal health responsibility. If the average purchase intent in the health routine integration condition is at least 10 points higher than in the personal health responsibility condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T2 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health routine integration. If neither condition shows a significant difference, the recommendation is to maintain the current B2B focus.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Health Routine
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious consumers (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a safety/peace-of-mind message about home CPR training (e.g., "Be prepared to save a life with home CPR training."). Group B receives a health/routine message (e.g., "Add home CPR training to your daily wellness routine."). Both groups see a product description of a portable home CPR kit and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").
X1.sample: 500 health-conscious consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (likelihood to purchase) for each messaging group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B because the safety message directly addresses life-saving motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A because the health/routine message aligns with existing health habits.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group A is at least 1.5 times the average WTP for Group B (i.e., WTP_A ≥ 1.5 × WTP_B), proceed to develop a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5, the health‑routine proposition is more likely to succeed and should be prioritized.

revisions.reason: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, messaging, or purchase behavior for home CPR training. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1, and the theory remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Invest in a safety/peace-of-mind consumer proposition for home CPR training, targeting health-conscious individuals who view CPR as a life-saving skill. The evidence shows a growing trend of bystanders administering CPR in home settings and Laerdal’s existing consumer product (CPR Anytime) demonstrates portability and family sharing, which aligns with the safety message.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers who already purchase fitness trackers, wellness apps, and home health devices, as well as families seeking peace of mind for home emergencies.
final.value_proposition: A portable home CPR training kit marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind solution, offering life-saving skills in the comfort of home, with optional subscription access to content and family sharing features.

final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for home CPR training and the size of the consumer market remain uncertain. The test results will determine whether the safety message drives purchase intent at a meaningful rate.
would_change_if: If the test shows the health/routine message achieving a 1.5  times higher willingness to pay than the safety message, the recommendation would shift to prioritize a health‑routine proposition.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Health Routine
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious consumers (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a safety/peace-of-mind message about home CPR training (e.g., "Be prepared to save a life with home CPR training."). Group B receives a health/routine message (e.g., "Add home CPR training to your daily wellness routine."). Both groups see a product description of a portable home CPR kit and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").
arguments.sample: 500 health-conscious consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (likelihood to purchase) for each messaging group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B because the safety message directly addresses life-saving motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A because the health/routine message aligns with existing health habits.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group A is at least 1.5 times the average WTP for Group B (i.e., WTP_A ≥ 1.5 × WTP_B), proceed to develop a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5, the health‑routine proposition is more likely to succeed and should be prioritized.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a safety/peace-of-mind consumer proposition for home CPR training, targeting health-conscious individuals who view CPR as a life-saving skill. The evidence shows a growing trend of bystanders administering CPR in home settings and Laerdal’s existing consumer product (CPR Anytime) demonstrates portability and family sharing, which aligns with the safety message.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: Group A (safety messaging) receives a home CPR training kit marketed as a safety product for family preparedness; Group B (digital integration) receives the same kit marketed as part of a digital health ecosystem (e.g., fitness app, insurance wellness program); Group C (control) receives no product. All participants are asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and to report their likelihood to purchase the product on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 500 health-conscious adults recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. Secondary measure: purchase intent (likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B and Group C.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A and Group C.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group A is at least 20% higher than Group B and at least 20% higher than Group C, proceed to develop a safety-focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% in either direction, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 10% in either direction, conduct a larger, more detailed test.

final.value_proposition: A portable, easy-to-use home CPR training kit that provides life-saving skills in as little as 20 minutes, marketed as a safety product for family preparedness, leveraging Laerdal’s brand trust in medical excellence.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (or a larger detailed test if the 20% difference is not met) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent for the safety-focused proposition.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay and purchase intent for a safety-focused home CPR training kit are uncertain; the test results will determine whether the investment is justified.
would_change_if: If the test shows a willingness to pay difference of less than 10% between the safety messaging and digital integration groups, indicating insufficient demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for home CPR training through digital health ecosystems, which would shift the recommendation toward a digital integration strategy.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).
5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan can capture value by pricing the product competitively, offering financial incentives (e.g., cashback or grant partnerships), and leveraging its existing distribution channels to reach consumers directly or through retailers.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Energy Savings vs Brand Trust
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of UK homeowners (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Condition A emphasizes energy savings and financial return on investment (ROI) of insulation. Condition B emphasizes brand trust, safety, and compliance with building regulations. After viewing the product description and price, participants indicate their likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale) and the maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 UK homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two message conditions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (likelihood to buy) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition B, because homeowners are motivated by financial ROI.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition A, because trust in the brand is the primary purchase driver.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 points (e.g., 60% vs 50%), we conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 10 points, we conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes energy savings and financial return on investment, leveraging Kingspan’s existing direct-to-consumer sales channel and retail partnerships to reach homeowners. Begin with a limited launch of a consumer‑facing insulation line, supported by targeted advertising and financial incentives to demonstrate ROI.
final.target_customer: UK homeowners and building owners who are motivated by reducing energy bills and improving home comfort.
final.value_proposition: A Kingspan consumer product that clearly communicates the financial benefits of insulation (lower heating costs) and is priced competitively, making it an affordable upgrade for homeowners.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (Condition A vs Condition B) to validate whether energy‑saving messaging drives higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than brand trust messaging.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no internal company data is available. The test budget and timeframe are assumptions, and the actual demand for a consumer proposition is unknown.
would_change_if: If the test shows Condition B (brand trust) generating at least 10 points higher purchase intent than Condition A, we would shift focus to brand trust as the primary driver and reconsider the consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference between the two conditions, we would recommend further market research before committing to a full consumer launch.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test: SEAI vs Premium Messaging
X1.method: Run a targeted online ad campaign with two versions: Version A presents Kingspan insulation as a SEAI‑backed, grant‑simplified solution; Version B presents the same product as a premium, high‑performance insulation with a price premium. Track click‑through and purchase conversion rates for each version.
X1.sample: 2,000 UK homeowners recruited via social media and email lists, split equally between Version A and Version B.
X1.measure: Conversion rate (purchases) and average willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Version A will achieve a higher conversion rate and WTP than Version B because homeowners are motivated by public funding and grant simplicity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Version B will achieve a higher conversion rate and WTP than Version A because homeowners value premium performance and are willing to pay more.

X1.decision_rule: If Version A’s conversion rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Version B, conclude T1 is supported. If Version B’s conversion rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Version A, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, neither theory is conclusively supported and further testing is needed.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes the SEAI grant‑simplified, government‑backed process, while also highlighting premium performance. Use the One Stop Shop model to capture volume sales and leverage public funding to lower customer upfront cost.
final.target_customer: UK homeowners undertaking home energy upgrades, particularly those who are aware of and eligible for SEAI grants or building code requirements.
final.value_proposition: A trusted, government‑backed insulation solution that simplifies the grant application process and delivers proven thermal performance, making upgrades affordable and compliant.
final.next_action: Run the proposed digital messaging test (Version A vs Version B) to measure conversion rates and willingness‑to‑pay, and use the results to decide whether to scale the premium positioning or maintain the grant‑focused approach.
final.uncertainty: The extent to which homeowners actually use the SEAI grant process and their willingness to pay a premium for performance remain uncertain. Additionally, the competitive landscape and retailer distribution could affect adoption.
would_change_if: If the test shows Version B (premium positioning) achieving a conversion rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Version A, we would shift focus to premium positioning.
If new evidence shows that homeowners are not aware of or do not trust the SEAI grant process, we would reconsider the grant‑focused proposition.

arguments.claim: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a reliable, government‑approved solution for energy efficiency, because they trust public funding (SEAI grants) and regulatory requirements to make upgrades affordable and compliant.
arguments.who_benefits: Kingspan gains volume sales and brand association with public energy‑efficiency programs.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: When homeowners receive SEAI grants or must meet building codes, they choose products that simplify the process and are backed by official recognition, reducing perceived risk and cost.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan sells through the SEAI One Stop Shop model, capturing margin on products while leveraging public funding to lower customer upfront cost.
assumptions: SEAI grants and building codes will continue to be available and enforceable in target markets.
Homeowners are aware of and trust the SEAI process.
Kingspan can integrate its products into the One Stop Shop workflow efficiently.
predictions: In regions with active SEAI grant programs, purchase intent for Kingspan insulation will be higher than for competitors without public backing.
Sales will correlate with the number of active SEAI grants in a region.
Customers will report lower perceived risk when purchasing through the One Stop Shop compared to self‑installing.

arguments.claim: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a premium, high‑performance product that offers superior thermal efficiency and durability, because they value long‑term value and are willing to pay a premium for proven quality.
arguments.who_benefits: Kingspan gains premium pricing and higher margins from consumers willing to pay more for perceived superior performance.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: When homeowners compare insulation options, they choose products that deliver measurable energy‑saving benefits and are backed by a reputation for durability, even if the upfront cost is higher.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan can price its premium product at a higher margin and sell through specialty channels or direct‑to‑consumer platforms that emphasize performance.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for thermal performance and durability.
Kingspan’s technical claims about insulation performance are credible and verifiable.
The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to homeowners.
predictions: In markets where energy‑efficiency is a key purchase driver, homeowners will show higher willingness to pay for Kingspan’s premium insulation compared to generic alternatives.
Sales of the premium product will be concentrated in regions where energy‑efficiency regulations or consumer awareness of performance are high.
Customers will report higher satisfaction with the product’s performance and durability compared to competitors.
